items.title: Fake Google Meet Updates, Abused RMM Tools, the AgtaBackup RAT Ecosystem & Campaign
items.summary: How a fraudulent video-conferencing update can turn legitimate remote administration software into an attacker-controlled foothold, potentially enabling a second-stage remote access Trojan Introduction A user attempts to access what appears to be a legitimate Google Meet session. Instead of joining a meeting, the user encounters a notification claiming that the installed version of Google Meet is no longer supported. The website offers an update that appears to be necessary before the meeting can continue. The user downloads a Windows Installer package named Google-Meet-0.1.76-x64.msi. What appears to be a routine software update is actually part of a potentially dangerous remote-access intrusion chain. The DFIR Report publicly disclosed indicators from an active investigation involving a counterfeit Google Meet website, a suspicious executable installed under a Google Meet-branded directory, and reported command-and-control (C2) infrastructure. Independent research from ScanMalware connects the same phishing infrastructure to a broader operation distributing remote monitoring and management (RMM) software. Related research published by Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 describes how similar access mechanisms are used to deploy a custom .NET remote access Trojan known as AgtaBackup RAT . The significance of this campaign extends beyond the malicious installer itself. Attackers are increasingly exploiting the trust organizations place in legitimate administrative software. Rather than immediately deploying an obviously malicious executable, an attacker can first establish remote access through an otherwise legitimate management platform. Once the endpoint is enrolled in an attacker-controlled management environment, the operator can use familiar system administration capabilities to execute commands, transfer files and deploy additional payloads. The crucial analytical distinction is that the reported Google Meet incident and the independently documented AgtaBackup RAT deployment are connected through campaign intelligence, but the public evidence does not establish that the particular victim received the second-stage RAT. This article reconstructs the reported intrusion, examines the technical mechanisms documented in the related campaign, and identifies detection opportunities for security operations centers using Microsoft Defender XDR, KQL, Sigma and Windows telemetry. What Do We Actually Know? The DFIR Report identified a suspicious executable installed at the following location: C:\Program Files\Google Meet\Agent\GoogleMeet.exe The reported SHA-256 hash is: b0d8467f2f2ed6a104e45b828b8f3c9637f8cd73a66166c3441aefb336906e95 The victim reportedly encountered a counterfeit Google Meet page hosted at 224meetgooglecomfskqcdzfcwh[.]com. The page claimed that the user's software was outdated and directed the user to download Google-Meet-0.1.76-x64.msi. Source of the screenshot Urlscan.io https://urlscan.io/screenshots/01a1baf8-b5ce-7019-826a-5a0462ae7711.png The investigation also identified cheapmovies[.]sbs, associated with 189[.]12[.]226[.]77:8443, as suspected command-and-control infrastructure. Screenshot cheapmovies[.]sbs VT 08.11.2026 These indicators provide a meaningful starting point for reconstructing the intrusion. The branded installation directory suggests application masquerading, while the reported C2 infrastructure provides an opportunity to correlate endpoint execution with suspicious external communications. However, the publicly disclosed indicators do not include the complete MSI contents, the executable’s Authenticode signature, its internal configuration, process execution telemetry or a packet capture. Consequently, the exact identity of GoogleMeet.exe remains unverified. Its filename and location are consistent with a disguised remote-access agent, but they do not prove that the executable itself is the AgtaBackup RAT. Sandbox RMM Agent disguised remote access agent error screenshot Indicators associated with the reported incident The IP address and domain should be treated as time-sensitive indicators. Port 8443 is commonly associated with alternative HTTPS services, but the port number alone does not establish whether this particular communication used HTTP, TLS or another protocol. The GoogleMeet.exe is also seen as opsrmm_agent.exe or ssl41.exe and ist not signed. Further names and file is not signed (VT) Reconstructing the Attack Chain Initial Contact and Social Engineering The attack begins by placing the victim in an environment that resembles a trusted video-conferencing application. The counterfeit Google Meet page uses recognizable branding and presents the user with a software compatibility problem. By claiming that the existing version is unsupported, the attacker creates a reason for the user to download and execute software outside the normal corporate deployment process. This approach exploits an everyday business workflow. Employees routinely join meetings, install collaboration software and respond to application update requests. The attacker does not need to exploit a browser vulnerability when the victim can be persuaded to execute an installer voluntarily. ScanMalware’s investigation adds another important dimension. Its reporting describes a broader phishing kit that includes counterfeit Google Meet, Zoom and Google Drive interfaces. ScanMalware Analysis (additional IOC can be found on the website) The research identifies tracking functionality that reports site visits and download activity to the operator. It also describes protective scripts that interfere with automated browsing and analysis. Such mechanisms can help attackers distinguish real visitors from security scanners, measure the effectiveness of their lures and maintain visibility into victim interaction. For defenders, this means that the phishing infrastructure is not merely a static website. It is part of an operational delivery system that can be adapted, rebranded and potentially reused across campaigns. MSI Delivery and Execution Following the fraudulent update instructions, the user downloads Google-Meet-0.1.76-x64.msi. Windows Installer packages are attractive delivery mechanisms because they are widely used for legitimate enterprise software deployment. They can install executables, write registry values, register services and execute installation actions under elevated permissions when authorized. A user who accepts an elevation prompt may therefore grant significant privileges to an installer whose origin has not been verified. Unit 42’s independently documented AgtaBackup campaign demonstrates this mechanism particularly clearly. In that campaign, fraudulent software pages distributed genuinely signed RMM installer packages, including products such as LogMeIn Resolve and ConnectWise ScreenConnect . The software itself could be legitimate, while its installation and enrollment were unauthorized. The installed RMM agent subsequently registered with infrastructure controlled through the attacker’s management account. For the specific Google Meet sample, analysts still need the original MSI to determine its embedded files, installation actions, signer, service registration and configuration. Particular attention should be paid to the CustomAction, File, Registry, ServiceInstall and InstallExecuteSequence MSI tables. These artifacts help establish whether the installer directly deploys a custom executable, repackages a legitimate RMM application, or performs additional actions during installation. Application Masquerading and Remote Connectivity The reported executable path is especially interesting: C:\Program Files\Google Meet\Agent\GoogleMeet.exe A directory under Program Files can make an installation appear more credible to an administrator reviewing the endpoint. The word Agent also resembles the naming convention of legitimate background management components. A deceptive installation path does not establish the executable’s underlying functionality, but it gives defenders a specific artifact to investigate. The reported C2 endpoint, 189[.]12[.]226[.]77:8443, provides a second investigative pivot. Defenders should determine whether the executable contacted this endpoint directly, whether another process established the connection, and whether the traffic was associated with remote management, payload retrieval or a custom control channel. The investigation should preserve DNS responses, TLS metadata when available, process-to-connection relationships, connection duration and transferred byte counts. It is also important to distinguish the suspected campaign C2 infrastructure from legitimate RMM vendor cloud infrastructure. An attacker-controlled RMM installation may communicate with the legitimate service provider rather than a suspicious domain. The malicious relationship exists because the endpoint is enrolled in an unauthorized management tenant, not necessarily because its network traffic uses an obviously malicious protocol. Establishing Remote Control Through RMM Software ScanMalware documents several remote-management products associated with the phishing-kit ecosystem, including rebranded Ops RMM agents, TraceRMM and self-hosted ScreenConnect installations. The research describes agents deployed under misleading application names and enrolled for operator control. Once such enrollment succeeds, the attacker may gain interactive capabilities that resemble those available to a legitimate administrator. Depending on the RMM product and its configuration, these capabilities may include remote terminal access, software deployment, file transfer, service management and unattended desktop control. This stage is operationally important because it creates an access mechanism that may survive the initial phishing session. The user can close the browser and return to normal work while the management agent continues operating in the background. In the related AgtaBackup campaign documented by Unit 42, the attacker used the installed RMM product to open a remote terminal on the victim system. The operator then used that access to initiate the next malware deployment stage. The public Google Meet indicators alone do not establish that an interactive RMM session occurred on the particular endpoint. Confirmation requires agent enrollment information, tenant identifiers, remote session records and endpoint process telemetry. PowerShell-Assisted Second-Stage Deployment Unit 42 documented a second stage in which an operator used the compromised RMM session to execute PowerShell commands. The commands downloaded another MSI package, AgtaBackupAgent.msi, from attacker-controlled infrastructure and invoked Windows Installer to install it silently. This sequence is significant because the malicious deployment originates from a process associated with remote administration. From the operating system’s perspective, the execution chain may resemble routine administrative activity. A defender who monitors only whether PowerShell or msiexec.exe is present will miss the more important question Which process initiated the command, under which security context, and why was the software installed? The same distinction applies to user consent. A user may have approved the initial RMM installation without knowing that the installed software would subsequently be used to deploy a separate remote access Trojan. The AgtaBackup deployment documented by Unit 42 is a related-campaign behavior, not a confirmed second stage of the specific Google Meet incident. Nevertheless, it provides a clear hypothesis that investigators can test through PowerShell telemetry, MSI installation records, process lineage, file creation events and network evidence. AgtaBackup RAT Installation and Persistence Unit 42 describes AgtaBackup RAT as a custom .NET 8.0 application capable of maintaining remote access and supporting multiple post-compromise functions. The documented installation places the primary executable under: C:\Program Files\Agta Backup\Credential Guard.exe The name Credential Guard.exe is particularly deceptive because it resembles a legitimate Windows security capability. The installation registers a Windows service named AgtaBackupAgentSvc, which executes under the LocalSystem security context. The RAT also uses two scheduled tasks, AgtaBackupAgentWatchdog and AgtaBackupAgentGuardian, to maintain persistence. According to Unit 42, these tasks execute at approximately one-minute intervals and can restore the malicious service after it is stopped or removed. Additional artifacts are stored under C:\ProgramData\Agta Backup. The documented malware also uses restrictive Windows service security descriptors to limit visibility and management access for users outside the SYSTEM context. This creates a more resilient persistence mechanism than simply placing an executable in a startup directory. An administrator who discovers and terminates the service may not have removed the underlying recovery mechanism. Investigators should therefore examine the service, scheduled tasks, installation directory, recovery configuration and associated process execution together. Command and Control, Credential Access and Surveillance Unit 42’s analysis identifies multiple capabilities in AgtaBackup RAT that extend well beyond standard remote administration. The documented implementation supports HTTP check-ins, WebSocket-based communications, remote terminal execution, file transfer, browser credential access, screen capture and keylogging. The report describes an HTTP check-in interval of approximately two seconds and a WebSocket channel with periodic keep-alive traffic. A fallback mechanism can use TCP port 4080. These are characteristics of the analyzed AgtaBackup RAT family. They should not be assumed to describe the reported Google Meet executable or the 8443 endpoint. The malware can collect credentials and session-related information from several browsers, including Chrome, Edge, Firefox and other Chromium-based products. Its keylogging functionality uses an additional executable named Window Security Health Services.exe, which imitates Windows security-related naming conventions. Screen capture and hidden desktop capabilities give the operator additional opportunities to observe or interact with the compromised host without normal user visibility. These functions create risks to confidentiality and integrity. Stolen credentials and browser session material could enable further identity compromise, while the remote terminal and file-transfer capabilities could allow unauthorized modification or collection of sensitive information. No public case evidence currently establishes that these activities occurred on the specific Google Meet victim. Mapping the Observed and Related Behaviors The following mapping deliberately separates directly reported case behavior from techniques documented in related AgtaBackup operations. Overview Behavioral Mapping (picture AI-created own OSINT/Malware Analyst) This mapping is intended to guide collection and detection engineering rather than establish a precise technique count for the reported incident. A technique documented in related malware research is not automatically evidence that the technique occurred on every endpoint associated with the wider campaign. The most important behavioral sequence for detection engineering is the movement from a deceptive software installation to persistent remote access and subsequent privileged activity. MITRE ATT&CK detection strategy DET0496 provides a relevant model for correlating remote-access tool execution, persistence, external communications and interactive operator actions. Log Sources and Mutuable Elements detecting RMM-Tools in Windows, detection strategy DET0496 Detection Engineering -Turning the Attack Chain Into SOC Analytics The campaign illustrates why detection strategies should combine indicators of compromise with behavior-based analytics. Detection Opportunity 1 - Microsoft Defender XDR KQL — Exact IOC Hunting The following query searches Microsoft Defender XDR advanced hunting tables for the reported case indicators. let startTime = datetime(2026-10-21); let targetHash = "b0d8467f2f2ed6a104e45b828b8f3c9637f8cd73a66166c3441aefb336906e95"; let lureDomain = "224meetgooglecomfskqcdzfcwh.com"; let c2Domain = "cheapmovies.sbs"; let c2IP = "189.12.226.77"; union isfuzzy=true ( DeviceFileEvents | where Timestamp >= startTime | where SHA256 =~ targetHash or FileName =~ "Google-Meet-0.1.76-x64.msi" or FolderPath endswith @"\Google Meet\Agent\GoogleMeet.exe" | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Evidence="File", Detail=FolderPath ), ( DeviceProcessEvents | where Timestamp >= startTime | where SHA256 =~ targetHash or ProcessCommandLine contains "Google-Meet-0.1.76-x64.msi" or FolderPath endswith @"\Google Meet\Agent\GoogleMeet.exe" | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Evidence="Process", Detail=ProcessCommandLine ), ( DeviceNetworkEvents | where Timestamp >= startTime | where RemoteIP == c2IP or RemoteUrl contains lureDomain or RemoteUrl contains c2Domain | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Evidence="Network", Detail=strcat( RemoteIP, ":", tostring(RemotePort), " ", RemoteUrl ) ) | order by Timestamp desc This query provides an initial retrospective hunt. The October 21 starting date reflects the beginning of the documented ScanMalware hunt period rather than a proven victim compromise date. Organizations should adapt the time range to their available telemetry retention. A network indicator match should be correlated with process activity and endpoint context before it is treated as evidence of a successful compromise. Detection Opportunity 2 - Microsoft Defender XDR KQL — Suspicious Operator Activity The next query investigates command interpreters and system management utilities launched by the reported Google Meet-branded executable. It also searches for process commands referencing known AgtaBackup artifacts. DeviceProcessEvents | where Timestamp > ago(45d) | where FileName in~ ( "powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe", "cmd.exe", "msiexec.exe", "sc.exe", "schtasks.exe" ) | where InitiatingProcessFolderPath endswith @"\Google Meet\Agent\GoogleMeet.exe" or ProcessCommandLine contains "AgtaBackupAgent.msi" or ProcessCommandLine contains "AgtaBackupAgentSvc" or ProcessCommandLine contains "AgtaBackupAgentWatchdog" or ProcessCommandLine contains "AgtaBackupAgentGuardian" | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine | order by Timestamp desc This query addresses two investigative questions. First, has the disguised Google Meet executable launched administrative tools that could indicate remote operator activity? Second, have any endpoint processes referenced artifacts associated with the separately documented AgtaBackup RAT? A positive result warrants examination of the full process tree, including any intermediate service or management processes. The query will not identify remote actions whose process lineage does not directly expose the Google Meet executable or whose commands do not contain the selected artifact names. The hunting logic should be extended to RMM-specific processes, tenant information and vendor audit records where these data sources are available. Detection Opportunity 3 - Sigma Rule — Suspicious Google Meet Agent Execution The following Sigma rule detects either execution from the reported Google Meet-branded agent path or an MSI installation command referencing the known installer name. title: Suspicious Google Meet Branded Agent Execution id: f8716f1e-3763-4b4d-a03e-667199cf8d1c status: experimental description: > Detects execution from the Google Meet agent path or installation of the MSI associated with the reported phishing incident. logsource: category: process_creation product: windows detection: selection_agent: Image|endswith: '\Google Meet\Agent\GoogleMeet.exe' selection_installer: Image|endswith: '\msiexec.exe' CommandLine|contains: 'Google-Meet-0.1.76-x64.msi' condition: selection_agent or selection_installer falsepositives: - Internally approved software using matching paths - Security testing reproducing the reported indicators level: high tags: - attack.t1036 - attack.t1204.002 The detection is specific to the reported case artifacts. A differently named installer or renamed executable may evade it. Detection Opportunity 4 — Sigma Rule — AgtaBackup Service Creation The following rule focuses on the second-stage persistence artifacts documented by Unit 42. It uses Windows System Event ID 7045, which records the installation of a new service. title: AgtaBackup RAT Service Installation id: a37d9e84-742c-4b47-9b0a-57e46190c8e2 status: experimental description: > Detects Windows service installation associated with the documented AgtaBackup RAT. logsource: product: windows service: system detection: selection_event: EventID: 7045 selection_name: ServiceName: 'AgtaBackupAgentSvc' selection_path: ImagePath|contains: '\Agta Backup\' condition: > selection_event and (selection_name or selection_path) falsepositives: - Authorized testing with AgtaBackup artifacts level: critical tags: - attack.t1543.003 This rule should be implemented with the understanding that service names and executable locations are changeable. The documented AgtaBackup service name is a high-value family-specific indicator, but its absence does not eliminate the possibility of unauthorized remote access. Analysts should also inspect Sysmon Event ID 13 for registry modifications, Windows Security Event ID 4698 for scheduled task creation, and PowerShell Script Block Logging Event ID 4104 where available. Detection Opportunity 5 — Behavioral Correlation Instead of Static Indicators The strongest detection strategy combines several events that may be individually legitimate. For example, a recently downloaded conferencing installer followed by the registration of an unfamiliar remote-management service deserves additional scrutiny. If the same endpoint subsequently initiates external management connections, launches PowerShell from an RMM process context and installs a second MSI package, the overall sequence becomes significantly more suspicious. This logic aligns with MITRE’s behavior-chain detection approach for remote-access tools. A practical SOC correlation should incorporate several conditions: The endpoint executes an installer obtained from a browser download or user-controlled directory. The installer creates or enables a remote-management agent that is not included in the organization’s approved RMM inventory. The agent communicates with a newly observed management tenant or unfamiliar external control infrastructure. The agent or its associated service initiates PowerShell, cmd.exe, msiexec.exe or another administrative utility. The subsequent activity creates persistence, transfers another executable or accesses sensitive credential-related data. Not every event will be observable in every environment. Endpoint process telemetry may show software execution without revealing the remote management tenant, while the vendor’s management console may record remote sessions that are not apparent in ordinary network logs. Effective detection therefore requires combining EDR, identity, software inventory, network and RMM administrative evidence. Forensic Investigation — Establishing Which Stages Actually Occurred When the reported indicators are discovered, investigators should reconstruct the intrusion before assigning the endpoint to the full AgtaBackup infection chain. The original MSI and installed executable should be preserved and analyzed. Their hashes, Authenticode signatures, certificate chains, PE metadata and installation actions may identify whether the payload is a legitimate RMM client, a repackaged application or custom malware. Windows Installer logs, Amcache, Prefetch and EDR telemetry can help determine whether the MSI executed and which components were installed. Investigators should reconstruct the process sequence beginning with the browser download and continuing through msiexec.exe, service creation, agent execution and any later administrative commands. The RMM configuration is particularly important. An attacker-controlled tenant identifier or a documented unauthorized remote session may provide stronger evidence of malicious control than a suspicious filename alone. For possible AgtaBackup deployment, the investigation should also search for AgtaBackupAgentSvc, the two recovery tasks, the associated installation directories and environment variables such as AGENT_CHECKIN_URL. The presence of AGENT_CHECKIN_SECRET should be handled carefully because it may contain sensitive enrollment material. Where browser credential access or session theft is suspected, the investigation must extend beyond the original endpoint. Identity provider logs, unusual sign-ins, session activity and access to sensitive services may reveal the consequences of compromised credentials. Finally, analysts should distinguish the absence of recorded evidence from evidence that a stage did not occur. Missing telemetry, limited retention or incomplete endpoint coverage may prevent a definitive conclusion. From Individual Indicators to Campaign Infrastructure ScanMalware’s reporting identifies additional infrastructure associated with the wider phishing-kit cluster. Examples include get-googlemeet[.]com, us06webzoomus2fj2f830440905293[.]com, alertbot-lake.vercel.app, relay.autoskreenllc.one and cheapmovellc[.]com. The IOC can support infrastructure clustering through historical DNS records, web scans, hosting relationships, common tracking code and repeated delivery behavior. The distinction matters because a phishing operation may change its visible brand without changing its underlying infrastructure or tracking functionality. ScanMalware specifically emphasizes that operator-specific installer builds can produce changing hashes, while components of the phishing kit and associated servers may remain recognizable. This makes kit-level detection valuable for identifying related activity beyond one executable. However, shared infrastructure does not automatically establish a single individual operator. Hosting reuse, shared tooling, reseller services or common administration infrastructure can produce apparent relationships between otherwise distinct activities. Campaign attribution therefore requires corroboration across multiple independent evidence sources. Defensive Priorities and Courses of Action Organizations should treat a confirmed installation of the reported agent as a potential unauthorized remote-access incident until its purpose and control relationship are established. The first priority is to determine whether the endpoint has active remote-control connectivity and preserve relevant forensic evidence before removing suspicious components. The second priority is to identify all remote-management software installed on the host and determine which tenants, accounts and management servers control those agents. The third priority is to inspect the endpoint for second-stage malware, especially services, scheduled tasks, PowerShell activity and files associated with the AgtaBackup RAT family. If credential or session theft is supported by evidence, identity remediation must accompany endpoint containment. Rebuilding a workstation will not invalidate credentials or tokens already stolen from it. At the enterprise level, defenders should maintain an approved RMM inventory, restrict unauthorized software installation through application control, and alert on new remote-management enrollment that does not match the organization’s administrative baseline. Detection engineering should prioritize process ancestry and multi-stage behavior over isolated malicious filenames. The most useful outcome of the investigation is establishing how the access was obtained, whether an external operator controlled the endpoint, what actions the operator performed and whether the intrusion extended into additional systems or identities. Why This Intrusion Model Matters This case reflects a broader challenge for modern security operations. Many defensive controls rely on distinctions between legitimate software and malicious software. Attackers increasingly exploit the fact that legitimate tools can perform activities that would otherwise be associated with malware. An RMM platform is designed to execute commands, install software and manage endpoints remotely. These capabilities are not malicious by themselves. They become dangerous when an attacker controls the management account or enrolls an endpoint without authorization. This creates an attribution and detection problem. A valid digital signature establishes information about a binary’s signing identity and integrity. It does not establish that the person deploying the software has a legitimate business purpose or that the management tenant is trustworthy. The use of a counterfeit conferencing website adds a human dimension to the attack. Rather than forcing access through a technical vulnerability, the operator creates a situation in which the victim is motivated to initiate the installation. The attacker’s opportunity comes from the interaction of social engineering, trusted software distribution and permissive remote-administration capabilities. Microsoft has independently documented similar abuse of legitimate RMM products in other phishing campaigns. That research provides additional context for the defensive problem, although it should not be interpreted as attribution of the Google Meet incident to those operators. Conclusion The Real Threat Is the Remote Access Established After the Download The fake Google Meet incident demonstrates how an ordinary collaboration workflow can become a route to unauthorized endpoint control. The reported evidence identifies a counterfeit update page, a downloaded MSI package, a Google Meet-branded executable and suspicious command-and-control infrastructure. ScanMalware’s independent research connects those indicators to a wider phishing-kit ecosystem designed to distribute remote-management agents. Unit 42’s research demonstrates how related operations can use such access to deploy AgtaBackup RAT, establish service-based persistence, maintain recovery mechanisms and conduct interactive post-compromise activities. The most important conclusion is not that every fake meeting installer necessarily delivers AgtaBackup RAT. It is that a deceptive software update can establish remote access that allows the attacker to decide what happens next. For defenders, that changes the detection priority. The most valuable telemetry is not necessarily the moment an executable first appears on disk. It may be the moment an unfamiliar management agent becomes enrolled, initiates its first external session or launches administrative commands that have no legitimate operational explanation. Static IOCs remain useful for identifying known activity, but they must be complemented by behavioral correlations across installation, persistence, remote control and secondary execution. The public evidence does not yet establish the full compromise sequence or final impact for the particular Google Meet victim. Those conclusions require original binaries, host telemetry, remote session records and network evidence. Nevertheless, the combined research provides a strong basis for proactive hunting. The defensive objective should be to recognize unauthorized remote administration before it becomes an enduring foothold for credential theft, information collection or additional malware deployment. Ultimately, the danger is not limited to a counterfeit Google Meet installer. It lies in the attacker’s ability to turn familiar and trusted administrative functionality into an invisible extension of the intrusion. The IP address and domain should be treated as time-sensitive indicators. Port 8443 is commonly associated with alternative HTTPS services, but the port number alone does not establish whether this particular communication used HTTP, TLS or another protocol.

The GoogleMeet.exe is also seen as opsrmm_agent.exe or ssl41.exe and ist not signed.

Further names and file is not signed (VT)Reconstructing the Attack ChainInitial Contact and Social Engineering

The attack begins by placing the victim in an environment that resembles a trusted video-conferencing application.

The counterfeit Google Meet page uses recognizable branding and presents the user with a software compatibility problem. By claiming that the existing version is unsupported, the attacker creates a reason for the user to download and execute software outside the normal corporate deployment process.

This approach exploits an everyday business workflow. Employees routinely join meetings, install collaboration software and respond to application update requests.

The attacker does not need to exploit a browser vulnerability when the victim can be persuaded to execute an installer voluntarily.

ScanMalware’s investigation adds another important dimension. Its reporting describes a broader phishing kit that includes counterfeit Google Meet, Zoom and Google Drive interfaces.

ScanMalware Analysis (additional IOC can be found on the website)

The research identifies tracking functionality that reports site visits and download activity to the operator. It also describes protective scripts that interfere with automated browsing and analysis.

Such mechanisms can help attackers distinguish real visitors from security scanners, measure the effectiveness of their lures and maintain visibility into victim interaction.

For defenders, this means that the phishing infrastructure is not merely a static website. It is part of an operational delivery system that can be adapted, rebranded and potentially reused across campaigns.

MSI Delivery and Execution

Following the fraudulent update instructions, the user downloads Google-Meet-0.1.76-x64.msi.

Windows Installer packages are attractive delivery mechanisms because they are widely used for legitimate enterprise software deployment. They can install executables, write registry values, register services and execute installation actions under elevated permissions when authorized.

A user who accepts an elevation prompt may therefore grant significant privileges to an installer whose origin has not been verified.

Unit 42’s independently documented AgtaBackup campaign demonstrates this mechanism particularly clearly. In that campaign, fraudulent software pages distributed genuinely signed RMM installer packages, including products such as LogMeIn Resolve and ConnectWise ScreenConnect.

The software itself could be legitimate, while its installation and enrollment were unauthorized. The installed RMM agent subsequently registered with infrastructure controlled through the attacker’s management account.

For the specific Google Meet sample, analysts still need the original MSI to determine its embedded files, installation actions, signer, service registration and configuration.

Particular attention should be paid to the CustomAction, File, Registry, ServiceInstall and InstallExecuteSequence MSI tables.

These artifacts help establish whether the installer directly deploys a custom executable, repackages a legitimate RMM application, or performs additional actions during installation.

Application Masquerading and Remote Connectivity

The reported executable path is especially interesting:

C:\Program Files\Google Meet\Agent\GoogleMeet.exe

A directory under Program Files can make an installation appear more credible to an administrator reviewing the endpoint.

The word Agent also resembles the naming convention of legitimate background management components.

A deceptive installation path does not establish the executable’s underlying functionality, but it gives defenders a specific artifact to investigate.

The reported C2 endpoint, 189[.]12[.]226[.]77:8443, provides a second investigative pivot.

Defenders should determine whether the executable contacted this endpoint directly, whether another process established the connection, and whether the traffic was associated with remote management, payload retrieval or a custom control channel.

The investigation should preserve DNS responses, TLS metadata when available, process-to-connection relationships, connection duration and transferred byte counts.

It is also important to distinguish the suspected campaign C2 infrastructure from legitimate RMM vendor cloud infrastructure.

An attacker-controlled RMM installation may communicate with the legitimate service provider rather than a suspicious domain. The malicious relationship exists because the endpoint is enrolled in an unauthorized management tenant, not necessarily because its network traffic uses an obviously malicious protocol.

Establishing Remote Control Through RMM Software

ScanMalware documents several remote-management products associated with the phishing-kit ecosystem, including rebranded Ops RMM agents, TraceRMM and self-hosted ScreenConnect installations.

The research describes agents deployed under misleading application names and enrolled for operator control. Once such enrollment succeeds, the attacker may gain interactive capabilities that resemble those available to a legitimate administrator.

Depending on the RMM product and its configuration, these capabilities may include remote terminal access, software deployment, file transfer, service management and unattended desktop control.

This stage is operationally important because it creates an access mechanism that may survive the initial phishing session. The user can close the browser and return to normal work while the management agent continues operating in the background.

In the related AgtaBackup campaign documented by Unit 42, the attacker used the installed RMM product to open a remote terminal on the victim system. The operator then used that access to initiate the next malware deployment stage.

The public Google Meet indicators alone do not establish that an interactive RMM session occurred on the particular endpoint. Confirmation requires agent enrollment information, tenant identifiers, remote session records and endpoint process telemetry.

PowerShell-Assisted Second-Stage Deployment

Unit 42 documented a second stage in which an operator used the compromised RMM session to execute PowerShell commands.

The commands downloaded another MSI package, AgtaBackupAgent.msi, from attacker-controlled infrastructure and invoked Windows Installer to install it silently.

This sequence is significant because the malicious deployment originates from a process associated with remote administration. From the operating system’s perspective, the execution chain may resemble routine administrative activity.

A defender who monitors only whether PowerShell or msiexec.exe is present will miss the more important question

Which process initiated the command, under which security context, and why was the software installed?

The same distinction applies to user consent. A user may have approved the initial RMM installation without knowing that the installed software would subsequently be used to deploy a separate remote access Trojan.

The AgtaBackup deployment documented by Unit 42 is a related-campaign behavior, not a confirmed second stage of the specific Google Meet incident.

Nevertheless, it provides a clear hypothesis that investigators can test through PowerShell telemetry, MSI installation records, process lineage, file creation events and network evidence.

AgtaBackup RAT Installation and Persistence

Unit 42 describes AgtaBackup RAT as a custom .NET 8.0 application capable of maintaining remote access and supporting multiple post-compromise functions.

The documented installation places the primary executable under:

C:\Program Files\Agta Backup\Credential Guard.exe

The name Credential Guard.exe is particularly deceptive because it resembles a legitimate Windows security capability.

The installation registers a Windows service named AgtaBackupAgentSvc, which executes under the LocalSystem security context.

The RAT also uses two scheduled tasks, AgtaBackupAgentWatchdog and AgtaBackupAgentGuardian, to maintain persistence.

According to Unit 42, these tasks execute at approximately one-minute intervals and can restore the malicious service after it is stopped or removed.

Additional artifacts are stored under C:\ProgramData\Agta Backup.

The documented malware also uses restrictive Windows service security descriptors to limit visibility and management access for users outside the SYSTEM context.

This creates a more resilient persistence mechanism than simply placing an executable in a startup directory.

An administrator who discovers and terminates the service may not have removed the underlying recovery mechanism.

Investigators should therefore examine the service, scheduled tasks, installation directory, recovery configuration and associated process execution together.

Command and Control, Credential Access and Surveillance

Unit 42’s analysis identifies multiple capabilities in AgtaBackup RAT that extend well beyond standard remote administration.

The documented implementation supports HTTP check-ins, WebSocket-based communications, remote terminal execution, file transfer, browser credential access, screen capture and keylogging.

The report describes an HTTP check-in interval of approximately two seconds and a WebSocket channel with periodic keep-alive traffic. A fallback mechanism can use TCP port 4080.

These are characteristics of the analyzed AgtaBackup RAT family. They should not be assumed to describe the reported Google Meet executable or the 8443 endpoint.

The malware can collect credentials and session-related information from several browsers, including Chrome, Edge, Firefox and other Chromium-based products.

Its keylogging functionality uses an additional executable named Window Security Health Services.exe, which imitates Windows security-related naming conventions.

Screen capture and hidden desktop capabilities give the operator additional opportunities to observe or interact with the compromised host without normal user visibility.

These functions create risks to confidentiality and integrity.

Stolen credentials and browser session material could enable further identity compromise, while the remote terminal and file-transfer capabilities could allow unauthorized modification or collection of sensitive information.

No public case evidence currently establishes that these activities occurred on the specific Google Meet victim.

Mapping the Observed and Related Behaviors

The following mapping deliberately separates directly reported case behavior from techniques documented in related AgtaBackup operations.

Overview Behavioral Mapping (picture AI-created own OSINT/Malware Analyst)

This mapping is intended to guide collection and detection engineering rather than establish a precise technique count for the reported incident.

A technique documented in related malware research is not automatically evidence that the technique occurred on every endpoint associated with the wider campaign.

The most important behavioral sequence for detection engineering is the movement from a deceptive software installation to persistent remote access and subsequent privileged activity.

MITRE ATT&CK detection strategy DET0496 provides a relevant model for correlating remote-access tool execution, persistence, external communications and interactive operator actions.

Log Sources and Mutuable Elements detecting RMM-Tools in Windows, detection strategy DET0496Detection Engineering -Turning the Attack Chain Into SOC Analytics

The campaign illustrates why detection strategies should combine indicators of compromise with behavior-based analytics.

Detection Opportunity 1 - Microsoft Defender XDR KQL — Exact IOC Hunting

The following query searches Microsoft Defender XDR advanced hunting tables for the reported case indicators.

let startTime = datetime(2026-10-21);
let targetHash =
    "b0d8467f2f2ed6a104e45b828b8f3c9637f8cd73a66166c3441aefb336906e95";
let lureDomain = "224meetgooglecomfskqcdzfcwh.com";
let c2Domain = "cheapmovies.sbs";
let c2IP = "189.12.226.77";
union isfuzzy=true
(
    DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp >= startTime
    | where SHA256 =~ targetHash
        or FileName =~ "Google-Meet-0.1.76-x64.msi"
        or FolderPath endswith
            @"\Google Meet\Agent\GoogleMeet.exe"
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName,
        Evidence="File",
        Detail=FolderPath
),
(
    DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp >= startTime
    | where SHA256 =~ targetHash
        or ProcessCommandLine contains
            "Google-Meet-0.1.76-x64.msi"
        or FolderPath endswith
            @"\Google Meet\Agent\GoogleMeet.exe"
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName,
        Evidence="Process",
        Detail=ProcessCommandLine
),
(
    DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp >= startTime
    | where RemoteIP == c2IP
        or RemoteUrl contains lureDomain
        or RemoteUrl contains c2Domain
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName,
        Evidence="Network",
        Detail=strcat(
            RemoteIP, ":",
            tostring(RemotePort), " ",
            RemoteUrl
        )
)
| order by Timestamp desc

This query provides an initial retrospective hunt. The October 21 starting date reflects the beginning of the documented ScanMalware hunt period rather than a proven victim compromise date. Organizations should adapt the time range to their available telemetry retention.

A network indicator match should be correlated with process activity and endpoint context before it is treated as evidence of a successful compromise.

Detection Opportunity 2 - Microsoft Defender XDR KQL — Suspicious Operator Activity

The next query investigates command interpreters and system management utilities launched by the reported Google Meet-branded executable. It also searches for process commands referencing known AgtaBackup artifacts.

DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(45d)
| where FileName in~ (
    "powershell.exe",
    "pwsh.exe",
    "cmd.exe",
    "msiexec.exe",
    "sc.exe",
    "schtasks.exe"
)
| where
    InitiatingProcessFolderPath endswith
        @"\Google Meet\Agent\GoogleMeet.exe"
    or ProcessCommandLine contains
        "AgtaBackupAgent.msi"
    or ProcessCommandLine contains
        "AgtaBackupAgentSvc"
    or ProcessCommandLine contains
        "AgtaBackupAgentWatchdog"
    or ProcessCommandLine contains
        "AgtaBackupAgentGuardian"
| project
    Timestamp,
    DeviceName,
    AccountName,
    FileName,
    FolderPath,
    ProcessCommandLine,
    InitiatingProcessFileName,
    InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
    InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

This query addresses two investigative questions.

  • First, has the disguised Google Meet executable launched administrative tools that could indicate remote operator activity?
  • Second, have any endpoint processes referenced artifacts associated with the separately documented AgtaBackup RAT?

A positive result warrants examination of the full process tree, including any intermediate service or management processes. The query will not identify remote actions whose process lineage does not directly expose the Google Meet executable or whose commands do not contain the selected artifact names.

The hunting logic should be extended to RMM-specific processes, tenant information and vendor audit records where these data sources are available.

Detection Opportunity 3 - Sigma Rule — Suspicious Google Meet Agent Execution

The following Sigma rule detects either execution from the reported Google Meet-branded agent path or an MSI installation command referencing the known installer name.

title: Suspicious Google Meet Branded Agent Execution
id: f8716f1e-3763-4b4d-a03e-667199cf8d1c
status: experimental
description: >
  Detects execution from the Google Meet agent
  path or installation of the MSI associated
  with the reported phishing incident.
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_agent:
    Image|endswith: '\Google Meet\Agent\GoogleMeet.exe'
  selection_installer:
    Image|endswith: '\msiexec.exe'
    CommandLine|contains: 'Google-Meet-0.1.76-x64.msi'
  condition: selection_agent or selection_installer
falsepositives:
  - Internally approved software using matching paths
  - Security testing reproducing the reported indicators
level: high
tags:
  - attack.t1036
  - attack.t1204.002

The detection is specific to the reported case artifacts. A differently named installer or renamed executable may evade it.

Detection Opportunity 4 — Sigma Rule — AgtaBackup Service Creation

The following rule focuses on the second-stage persistence artifacts documented by Unit 42. It uses Windows System Event ID 7045, which records the installation of a new service.

title: AgtaBackup RAT Service Installation
id: a37d9e84-742c-4b47-9b0a-57e46190c8e2
status: experimental
description: >
  Detects Windows service installation
  associated with the documented AgtaBackup RAT.
logsource:
  product: windows
  service: system
detection:
  selection_event:
    EventID: 7045
  selection_name:
    ServiceName: 'AgtaBackupAgentSvc'
  selection_path:
    ImagePath|contains: '\Agta Backup\'
  condition: >
    selection_event and
    (selection_name or selection_path)
falsepositives:
  - Authorized testing with AgtaBackup artifacts
level: critical
tags:
  - attack.t1543.003

This rule should be implemented with the understanding that service names and executable locations are changeable. The documented AgtaBackup service name is a high-value family-specific indicator, but its absence does not eliminate the possibility of unauthorized remote access.

Analysts should also inspect Sysmon Event ID 13 for registry modifications, Windows Security Event ID 4698 for scheduled task creation, and PowerShell Script Block Logging Event ID 4104 where available.

Detection Opportunity 5 — Behavioral Correlation Instead of Static Indicators

The strongest detection strategy combines several events that may be individually legitimate. For example, a recently downloaded conferencing installer followed by the registration of an unfamiliar remote-management service deserves additional scrutiny.

If the same endpoint subsequently initiates external management connections, launches PowerShell from an RMM process context and installs a second MSI package, the overall sequence becomes significantly more suspicious.

This logic aligns with MITRE’s behavior-chain detection approach for remote-access tools.

A practical SOC correlation should incorporate several conditions:

  1. The endpoint executes an installer obtained from a browser download or user-controlled directory.
  2. The installer creates or enables a remote-management agent that is not included in the organization’s approved RMM inventory.
  3. The agent communicates with a newly observed management tenant or unfamiliar external control infrastructure.
  4. The agent or its associated service initiates PowerShell, cmd.exe, msiexec.exe or another administrative utility.
  5. The subsequent activity creates persistence, transfers another executable or accesses sensitive credential-related data.

Not every event will be observable in every environment. Endpoint process telemetry may show software execution without revealing the remote management tenant, while the vendor’s management console may record remote sessions that are not apparent in ordinary network logs.

Effective detection therefore requires combining EDR, identity, software inventory, network and RMM administrative evidence.

Forensic Investigation — Establishing Which Stages Actually Occurred

When the reported indicators are discovered, investigators should reconstruct the intrusion before assigning the endpoint to the full AgtaBackup infection chain.

The original MSI and installed executable should be preserved and analyzed. Their hashes, Authenticode signatures, certificate chains, PE metadata and installation actions may identify whether the payload is a legitimate RMM client, a repackaged application or custom malware.

Windows Installer logs, Amcache, Prefetch and EDR telemetry can help determine whether the MSI executed and which components were installed.

Investigators should reconstruct the process sequence beginning with the browser download and continuing through msiexec.exe, service creation, agent execution and any later administrative commands.

The RMM configuration is particularly important. An attacker-controlled tenant identifier or a documented unauthorized remote session may provide stronger evidence of malicious control than a suspicious filename alone.

For possible AgtaBackup deployment, the investigation should also search for AgtaBackupAgentSvc, the two recovery tasks, the associated installation directories and environment variables such as AGENT_CHECKIN_URL.

The presence of AGENT_CHECKIN_SECRET should be handled carefully because it may contain sensitive enrollment material.

Where browser credential access or session theft is suspected, the investigation must extend beyond the original endpoint. Identity provider logs, unusual sign-ins, session activity and access to sensitive services may reveal the consequences of compromised credentials.

Finally, analysts should distinguish the absence of recorded evidence from evidence that a stage did not occur. Missing telemetry, limited retention or incomplete endpoint coverage may prevent a definitive conclusion.

From Individual Indicators to Campaign Infrastructure

ScanMalware’s reporting identifies additional infrastructure associated with the wider phishing-kit cluster.

Examples include get-googlemeet[.]com, us06webzoomus2fj2f830440905293[.]com, alertbot-lake.vercel.app, relay.autoskreenllc.one and cheapmovellc[.]com.

The IOC can support infrastructure clustering through historical DNS records, web scans, hosting relationships, common tracking code and repeated delivery behavior.

The distinction matters because a phishing operation may change its visible brand without changing its underlying infrastructure or tracking functionality.

ScanMalware specifically emphasizes that operator-specific installer builds can produce changing hashes, while components of the phishing kit and associated servers may remain recognizable.

This makes kit-level detection valuable for identifying related activity beyond one executable.

However, shared infrastructure does not automatically establish a single individual operator. Hosting reuse, shared tooling, reseller services or common administration infrastructure can produce apparent relationships between otherwise distinct activities.

Campaign attribution therefore requires corroboration across multiple independent evidence sources.

Defensive Priorities and Courses of Action

Organizations should treat a confirmed installation of the reported agent as a potential unauthorized remote-access incident until its purpose and control relationship are established.

  • The first priority is to determine whether the endpoint has active remote-control connectivity and preserve relevant forensic evidence before removing suspicious components.
  • The second priority is to identify all remote-management software installed on the host and determine which tenants, accounts and management servers control those agents.
  • The third priority is to inspect the endpoint for second-stage malware, especially services, scheduled tasks, PowerShell activity and files associated with the AgtaBackup RAT family.
If credential or session theft is supported by evidence, identity remediation must accompany endpoint containment. Rebuilding a workstation will not invalidate credentials or tokens already stolen from it.

At the enterprise level, defenders should maintain an approved RMM inventory, restrict unauthorized software installation through application control, and alert on new remote-management enrollment that does not match the organization’s administrative baseline.

Detection engineering should prioritize process ancestry and multi-stage behavior over isolated malicious filenames.

The most useful outcome of the investigation is establishing how the access was obtained, whether an external operator controlled the endpoint, what actions the operator performed and whether the intrusion extended into additional systems or identities.

Why This Intrusion Model Matters

This case reflects a broader challenge for modern security operations. Many defensive controls rely on distinctions between legitimate software and malicious software. Attackers increasingly exploit the fact that legitimate tools can perform activities that would otherwise be associated with malware.

An RMM platform is designed to execute commands, install software and manage endpoints remotely. These capabilities are not malicious by themselves. They become dangerous when an attacker controls the management account or enrolls an endpoint without authorization.

This creates an attribution and detection problem. A valid digital signature establishes information about a binary’s signing identity and integrity. It does not establish that the person deploying the software has a legitimate business purpose or that the management tenant is trustworthy.

The use of a counterfeit conferencing website adds a human dimension to the attack. Rather than forcing access through a technical vulnerability, the operator creates a situation in which the victim is motivated to initiate the installation.

The attacker’s opportunity comes from the interaction of social engineering, trusted software distribution and permissive remote-administration capabilities.

Microsoft has independently documented similar abuse of legitimate RMM products in other phishing campaigns. That research provides additional context for the defensive problem, although it should not be interpreted as attribution of the Google Meet incident to those operators.

ConclusionThe Real Threat Is the Remote Access Established After the Download

The fake Google Meet incident demonstrates how an ordinary collaboration workflow can become a route to unauthorized endpoint control.

The reported evidence identifies a counterfeit update page, a downloaded MSI package, a Google Meet-branded executable and suspicious command-and-control infrastructure.

ScanMalware’s independent research connects those indicators to a wider phishing-kit ecosystem designed to distribute remote-management agents.

Unit 42’s research demonstrates how related operations can use such access to deploy AgtaBackup RAT, establish service-based persistence, maintain recovery mechanisms and conduct interactive post-compromise activities.

The most important conclusion is not that every fake meeting installer necessarily delivers AgtaBackup RAT. It is that a deceptive software update can establish remote access that allows the attacker to decide what happens next.

For defenders, that changes the detection priority. The most valuable telemetry is not necessarily the moment an executable first appears on disk. It may be the moment an unfamiliar management agent becomes enrolled, initiates its first external session or launches administrative commands that have no legitimate operational explanation.

Static IOCs remain useful for identifying known activity, but they must be complemented by behavioral correlations across installation, persistence, remote control and secondary execution.

The public evidence does not yet establish the full compromise sequence or final impact for the particular Google Meet victim. Those conclusions require original binaries, host telemetry, remote session records and network evidence. Nevertheless, the combined research provides a strong basis for proactive hunting.

The defensive objective should be to recognize unauthorized remote administration before it becomes an enduring foothold for credential theft, information collection or additional malware deployment.

Ultimately, the danger is not limited to a counterfeit Google Meet installer. It lies in the attacker’s ability to turn familiar and trusted administrative functionality into an invisible extension of the intrusion.

items.title: Lima v2.3: Native on Windows, VMnet on Linux, and menu TUI
items.summary: Back in July with v2.2 , we added support for Windows guests. On November 6, we shipped v2.3 of Lima and now it runs without extra dependencies on Windows: VMs start through the same Host Compute System that powers WSL2, without QEMU and without a Unix toolchain. On Linux, VMs are getting the “ real IP address” networking that Mac users have had through ` socket_vmnet `. And on every host, managing your VMs gets friendlier with a new terminal UI . What is Lima? Lima (Linux Machines) is a command-line tool to launch local virtual machines. Originally focused on running containers on a laptop and promoting containerd to Mac users, Lima joined the CNCF as a Sandbox project in September 2022 and was promoted to Incubating in October 2025. Today, Lima supports a wide variety of non-container workloads, non-macOS hosts, non-Linux guests and robust AI sandboxing. If you are using Homebrew, Lima can be installed using: brew install lima If you are on Windows, Lima can be installed through PowerShell using: winget install Lima.Lima For other installation methods, see https://lima-vm.io/docs/installation/ . Updates in v2.3 Windows hosts: the HCS driver (experimental) Until now, Windows users who wanted Lima had two options: the ` wsl2 ` or QEMU driver. v2.3 adds a third, the new ` hcs ` driver . It talks directly to the Windows Host Compute System (HCS) API, the Windows virtualization layer that WSL2 is built on. In the v2.2 announcement, we said that our LFX mentorship would “explore and evaluate native virtualization support for Windows hosts”. A few weeks later, that research has become a working driver. Before you try it Enable virtualization on your machine. Add yourself to the ` Hyper-V Administrators ` group from an Administrator PowerShell, then restart your terminal: net localgroup "Hyper-V Administrators" /add Then run Lima from a shell: limactl start --vm-type hcs --plain --dns 8.8.8.8 lima Current limitations Only `plain` mode is supported. There are no file mounts and no dynamic port forwarding yet. Only one HCS instance can run at a time, because the HCN network subnet is fixed. A DNS server must be specified explicitly using the `–dns` flag. See the HCS driver docs for details. More Windows improvements Lima now recognizes Windows built-in SSH client, handles Windows paths correctly, and uses a matching mount server. ` limactl shell` , ` limactl copy `, and reverse-sshfs mounts work on a stock Windows install. If you install QEMU in its default location, Lima previously could not find it until you added ` %PROGRAMFILES%\QEMU ` to your ` PATH ` by hand. Lima now checks these common install directories automatically. The Windows guests introduced in v2.2 could boot, but you could not customize them at startup. They now have limited support for ` provision `. ` system `, ` user `, ` data ` and ` dependency ` scripts let you install software and configure the guest automatically. ` boot `, ` yq ` and `ansible` modes are not supported yet. See the Windows guest docs for details. Linux hosts: Real networking for VMs On macOS, ` socket_vmnet ` gives VMs an IP address that the host can reach directly. Linux had no equivalent, so the ` lima: shared `, ` lima: host ` and ` lima: bridged ` networks only worked on macOS. v2.3 introduces ` lima-privileged-net `, a small privileged helper for Linux hosts which: creates a Linux bridge for each network and assigns the gateway address, runs ` dnsmasq ` for DHCP and DNS, and adds NAT and forwarding rules for ` shared ` mode, creates one tap device per instance, gives it to the calling user, and attaches it to the bridge, removes the network again when the last instance leaves, and only ever touches interfaces that follow Lima’s naming scheme. One-time setup on Linux: the `sudoers` file Creating bridges and tap devices requires root, so there are two steps before your first start: Install Lima as root, and install ` dnsmasq `. ` limactl sudoers ` refuses to generate rules for a helper that isn’t root-owned. Generate and install the rules: limactl sudoers >etc_sudoers.d_lima less etc_sudoers.d_lima sudo install -o root -m 0440 etc_sudoers.d_lima /etc/sudoers.d/lima rm etc_sudoers.d_lima Then start an instance on a managed network: limactl start --network=lima:shared --vm-type=qemu See the Linux networking docs for details. macOS hosts: Give your VM a real disk With v2.3, Lima can now attach a block device (USB drive or an external SSD) to VZ guests, without going through a file share. In order for this feature to work, sudo privileges are required to configure it. Back in July with v2.2, we added support for Windows guests. On November 6, we shipped v2.3 of Lima and now it runs without extra dependencies on Windows: VMs start through the same Host Compute System that powers WSL2, without QEMU and without a Unix toolchain. On Linux, VMs are getting the “real IP address” networking that Mac users have had through `socket_vmnet`. And on every host, managing your VMs gets friendlier with a new terminal UI.

What is Lima?

Lima (Linux Machines) is a command-line tool to launch local virtual machines. Originally focused on running containers on a laptop and promoting containerd to Mac users, Lima joined the CNCF as a Sandbox project in September 2022 and was promoted to Incubating in October 2025. Today, Lima supports a wide variety of non-container workloads, non-macOS hosts, non-Linux guests and robust AI sandboxing.

If you are using Homebrew, Lima can be installed using:

brew install lima


If you are on Windows, Lima can be installed through PowerShell using:

winget install Lima.Lima

For other installation methods, see https://lima-vm.io/docs/installation/.

Updates in v2.3 Windows hosts: the HCS driver (experimental) 

Until now, Windows users who wanted Lima had two options: the `wsl2` or QEMU driver. v2.3 adds a third, the new `hcs` driver. It talks directly to the Windows Host Compute System (HCS) API, the Windows virtualization layer that WSL2 is built on. In the v2.2 announcement, we said that our LFX mentorship would “explore and evaluate native virtualization support for Windows hosts”. A few weeks later, that research has become a working driver. 

Before you try it
  1. Enable virtualization on your machine. 
  2. Add yourself to the `Hyper-V Administrators` group from an Administrator PowerShell, then restart your terminal:
net localgroup "Hyper-V Administrators"  /add
  1. Then run Lima from a shell:
limactl start --vm-type hcs --plain --dns 8.8.8.8
lima
Current limitations 
  • Only `plain` mode is supported. There are no file mounts and no dynamic port forwarding yet.
  • Only one HCS instance can run at a time, because the HCN network subnet is fixed.
  • A DNS server must be specified explicitly using the `–dns` flag.

See the HCS driver docs for details. 

More Windows improvements 
  • Lima now recognizes Windows built-in SSH client, handles Windows paths correctly, and uses a matching mount server. `limactl shell`, `limactl copy`, and reverse-sshfs mounts work on a stock Windows install.
  • If you install QEMU in its default location, Lima previously could not find it until you added `%PROGRAMFILES%\QEMU` to your `PATH` by hand. Lima now checks these common install directories automatically. 
  • The Windows guests introduced in v2.2 could boot, but you could not customize them at startup. They now have limited support for `provision`. `system`, `user`, `data` and `dependency` scripts let you install software and configure the guest automatically. `boot`, `yq` and `ansible` modes are not supported yet. See the Windows guest docs for details.
Linux hosts: Real networking for VMs

On macOS, `socket_vmnet` gives VMs an IP address that the host can reach directly. Linux had no equivalent, so the `lima: shared`, `lima: host` and `lima: bridged` networks only worked on macOS.

v2.3 introduces `lima-privileged-net`, a small privileged helper for Linux hosts which:

  • creates a Linux bridge for each network and assigns the gateway address, 
  • runs `dnsmasq` for DHCP and DNS, and adds NAT and forwarding rules for `shared` mode, 
  • creates one tap device per instance, gives it to the calling user, and attaches it to the bridge, 
  • removes the network again when the last instance leaves, and only ever touches interfaces that follow Lima’s naming scheme.
One-time setup on Linux: the `sudoers` file

Creating bridges and tap devices requires root, so there are two steps before your first start:

  1. Install Lima as root, and install `dnsmasq`. `limactl sudoers` refuses to generate rules for a helper that isn’t root-owned.
  2. Generate and install the rules:
limactl sudoers >etc_sudoers.d_lima
less etc_sudoers.d_lima
sudo install -o root -m 0440 etc_sudoers.d_lima /etc/sudoers.d/lima
rm etc_sudoers.d_lima

Then start an instance on a managed network:

limactl start --network=lima:shared --vm-type=qemu

See the Linux networking docs for details.

macOS hosts: Give your VM a real disk

With v2.3, Lima can now attach a block device (USB drive or an external SSD) to VZ guests, without going through a file share. In order for this feature to work, sudo privileges are required to configure it. 

One-time setup on macOS: the `sudoers` file

Opening a host disk requires root, so there are two steps before your first `–block-device` start:

  1. The helper and every directory above it must be root-owned. Typical Homebrew installs are user-writable, so extract the macOS release archive into `/opt/lima` and run `/opt/lima/bin/limactl` directly:As your regular user, generate the rule, review it, and install it:
    sudo install -d -o root -g wheel -m 0755 /opt/lima
sudo tar --no-same-owner -xzf lima-VERSION-Darwin-ARCH.tar.gz -C /opt/lima

    2. As your regular user, generate the rule, review it, and install it:

      limactl sudoers --block-device=/dev/disk4 >etc_sudoers.d_lima
less etc_sudoers.d_lima
visudo -cf etc_sudoers.d_lima
sudo install -o root -g wheel -m 0444 etc_sudoers.d_lima /etc/sudoers.d/lima
rm etc_sudoers.d_lima

      The rule only lets your user run the helper on that one device. When you regenerate the file, include every grant you want to keep, because installing it replaces the previous file.

      After these steps, then it’s a single flag:

      limactl start --vm-type=vz --block-device=/dev/disk4 template:default 

      Inside the guest, each device appears under `/dev/disk/by-id/virtio-` (for example `virtio-disk4`). From there you can partition, format and mount it as you like. You can repeat `--block-device` to attach more than one device.

      💡 If you don’t have a spare drive, you can also test with a RAM disk: `hdiutil attach -nomount ram://65536` 

      ⚠️ macOS mounts external drives automatically. Unmount the drive first (e.g. `diskutil unmountDisk /dev/disk4`, don’t eject it), or the VM fails to start with `resource busy`.

      Built with security in mind

      Giving a VM raw access to a disk is powerful, so it needs to be safe. An earlier implementation of this feature was reverted after a security report. The version in v2.3 was redesigned around a few principles:

      • Lima itself never opens the disk as root. A dedicated privileged helper, `lima-privileged-block-device`, does it instead. Lima refuses to use the helper unless it and every directory above it are owned by root and not writable by regular users. 
      • Access is granted per device, through a `sudoers` file generated by `limactl sudoers --block-device=/dev/diskN`. The helper only accepts real macOS disk device nodes, and only the ones listed in that file. You review the file, validate it with `visudo -cf`, and then install it yourself. Starting a VM never grants root access silently.
      • Instances that share a `LIMA_HOME’ lock the whole disk, including its raw and block aliases and partitions. This prevents two VMs from writing to the same disk.

       ⚠️ Never grant access to your boot or system disk. Never mount the same filesystem on the host and in a guest (or in two guests) at the same time. 

      The full setup guide is in the disk docs.

      More for macOS
      • Set `osOpts.Darwin.suppressFirstLoginSetup: true` and Lima pre-configures macOS guests so the first-login setup screens are skipped. This is useful for headless or automated VMs.
      • `audio.microphone: true` gives VZ guests a capture device in addition to speakers. It is opt-in, so macOS only asks for microphone permission when you enable it. 
      • `nestedVirtualization` now works with the HVF accelerator on aarch64 (requires QEMU 11.1 or later and macOS 15 or later). 
      • `limactl snapshot` now works with the krunkit driver while the instance is stopped. 
      `limactl menu`: a TUI for your VMs (experimental)

      If you prefer arrow keys to typing commands then v2.3 adds `limactl menu’, an interactive terminal UI for managing your Lima instances.

      limactl menu

      It lists your instances with color-coded status (running first), along with each instance’s VM type, architecture, CPUs and memory. Select an instance to:

      • open a shell,
      • start, stop or restart it,
      • view its info or port forwards,
      • protect or unprotect it,
      • delete it.

      Destructive actions ask for confirmation first. If you don’t have any instances yet, the menu offers to create one.

      Safer AI sandboxes

      As more people use Lima to run AI coding agents, v2.3 adds a few small but useful features for that use case:

      • Choose what the agent gets to see.`limactl shell --sync` copies your project into the VM so an agent can work on it, then asks you whether to sync the changes back. Until now, it copied everything, including secrets like `.env` files, your `.git` directory, and heavy folders like `node_modules`. The new `--sync-exclude` flag (repeatable, using rsync’s `--exclude` patterns) keeps them on the host:
      limactl shell --sync . --sync-exclude .git --sync-exclude node_modules default

      To keep the list with your project instead, add a `.limasyncignore` file to the directory you sync, with one pattern per line. 

      • By default, a guest can reach services listening on the host’s `127.0.0.1` through `host.lima.internal`. With the new `networkOpts.hostLoopback: false` (VZ only), those connections are refused immediately. This means a local database or dev server on your Mac stays out of reach of whatever is running in the VM. See the network docs for details.
      • Lima’s MCP tools now include `replace`. Agents can make targeted edits to files inside the guest instead of re-sending the whole file, which saves tokens and reduces the risk of accidental changes.

      For the complete list of changes, see the v2.3 milestone.

      Thank you, Mie!

      Mie Tokunaga (@mie313) has successfully completed the LFX Mentorship 2026 Term 2 program with Lima. Over the term she brought Windows guests to Lima in v2.2, and in v2.3 she added `provision` support for those guests, automatic `PATH` setup on Windows hosts, and the HCS driver. She did excellent work throughout the program, and it was a pleasure to work with her. Thank you, Mie, and congratulations! 🎉
